summary: Defines a one-way metric for packet duplication, when more than one copy of a sent packet arrives. It complements the earlier packet loss metric, which counts when none arrive.

eli5.summary: Normally one letter sent means one letter arrives, but sometimes two copies show up. This note defines how to measure how often that happens.

questions: what is the one-way packet duplication metric
packet duplication fraction vs replicated packet rate
subtitle: How to count the extra copies of a packet that show up when only one was sent.

tldr.problem: Packet loss already had a standard metric, but nothing measured the opposite case, where one packet is sent and several identical copies arrive.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5560 defines a per-packet arrival count and a duplication value (arrival count minus one), then builds Poisson-stream and periodic-stream samples and two summary statistics on top of them.
tldr.outcome: It gives measurement tools a shared definition of duplication so results from different implementations can be compared. It is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 6248.

today: RFC 5560 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 6248; it has not been obsoleted. Its metrics are registered in the IPPM Metrics Registry.

sections.title: Introduction and Motivation
sections.content:
RFC 5560 defines a metric for one-way packet duplication across Internet paths. It builds on the IP Performance Metrics (IPPM) framework in RFC 2330 and copies the structure of the one-way packet loss metric in RFC 2680. Readers are assumed to know both.

Normally one packet sent means exactly one copy arrives. The packet loss metric covers the case where it does not arrive within a reasonable time. This memo covers a third outcome: a single packet is sent but multiple copies arrive. Because the case is so close to packet loss, all the timing and accuracy considerations of RFC 2680 apply.

The document uses the RFC 2119 key words, but for measurement reasons: to make results from two implementations comparable and to flag cases where an implementation could disturb the network.
sections.eli5: Mail normally arrives once or not at all. This note is about the odd case where the same letter turns up more than once.

sections.title: Packet Arrival Count
sections.content:
The first building block is the singleton metric Type-P-one-way-packet-arrival-count. Its parameters are src and dst (IP addresses), T (the wire time of the packet at the source) and T0 (the maximum time to wait for a packet to arrive). The result is an integer.

Two packets count as identical only if both carry identical information fields, so a recipient could use either one with nothing lost, and both appear to come from the same host to the same destination. The value is the number of uncorrupted, identical copies received by dst in the interval [T, T+T0]. If nothing arrives in that interval the value is undefined, though applications MAY report an impossible value such as -1. A packet that is fragmented and never reassembled is deemed lost.

Several rules keep results honest. T0 SHOULD be long enough that an application could still use the packet. If the metric runs alongside the loss metric, T0 MUST be the same for both. Corrupted packets are not counted, and clocks at both ends have to be synchronized. An active measurement system MUST NOT send multiple packets with identical information fields, or every packet would be declared a duplicate.

The implementation MUST specify which fields it compares, because copies sent along different paths may differ in fields such as Time to Live. For IPv4 these usually include version, ihl, identification, src, dst, protocol and some or all upper-layer data. For IPv6 they usually include version, next header, source, destination and some or all upper-layer data. The text warns that the identification field may not be enough to tell packets apart, particularly at higher transmission speeds.

In a passive measurement system, a source that really sends two identical packets within the interval will be labeled a false-positive duplicate. The implementor must judge how likely that is.
sections.eli5: To count copies, first decide what makes two letters the same: same sender, same address, same words inside. Then count how many of those arrive before you stop waiting.

sections.title: The Duplication Singleton
sections.content:
The second singleton, Type-P-one-way-packet-duplication, uses the same four parameters (src, dst, T, T0) and also returns an integer. It counts the additional copies of one packet received in [T, T+T0].

The RFC states it as a simple relation: duplication equals the packet arrival count minus 1. One copy arriving gives 0. No copy arriving makes the value undefined, and an impossible value such as -1 MAY be reported instead.

This form is meant for applications that need to know about duplication of an individual packet. Methodology, errors and reporting follow the arrival-count section.
sections.eli5: Duplication is just the number of extra copies. One copy means zero extras, two copies means one extra.

sections.title: Streams of Test Packets
sections.content:
To measure duplication over time, the RFC defines two kinds of sample. Both take src, dst, a start time Ts, an end time Tf, the wait time T0 and a rate lambda in reciprocal seconds. The result is a sequence of pairs, each holding a send time T and the arrival count for the packet sent then. A sample with no pairs is empty.

The Poisson stream (Type-P-one-way-Packet-Duplication-Poisson-Stream) computes a pseudo-random Poisson process with average rate lambda and keeps the send times from Ts to Tf. Its methodology, errors and reporting refer to RFC 2680.

The periodic stream (Type-P-one-way-Packet-Duplication-Periodic-Stream) starts at Ts and sends at a constant rate lambda until Tf. Its methodology, errors and reporting refer to RFC 3432.
sections.eli5: Instead of testing one letter, you send a whole series, either at random moments or at steady beats, and write down how many copies of each one arrived.

sections.title: Summary Statistics
sections.content:
Two statistics summarize a stream. Both first remove pairs whose arrival count is undefined, and the application SHOULD report which sample it used as input. Either can be shown as a percentage.

Type-P-one-way-packet-duplication-fraction is the fraction of additional packets that arrived: the sum of the arrival counts divided by the number of pairs left, minus 1. In words, packets received over packets sent and not lost, minus 1. The RFC notes it is the equivalent of the Y.1540 IPDR.

Type-P-one-way-replicated-packet-rate is the fraction of packets duplicated one or more times: the number of pairs with an arrival count greater than 1, as a fraction of the pairs left. The RFC notes it is the equivalent of the Y.1540 RIPR.
sections.eli5: One number says how many extra copies there were overall. The other says what share of the letters got copied at all. You need both to see the whole picture.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC compares four cases for a stream of 4 packets, sent as (1, 2, 3, 4). In case 1 they arrive once each, so both statistics are 0. In case 2 every packet arrives twice, so both are 100%. In case 3 every packet arrives three times, so the duplication fraction is 200% while the replicated packet rate is still 100%. In case 4 the arrivals are (1, 1, 1, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4): half the packets are duplicated twice and half not at all.

Case 4 shows why both statistics are needed. Its duplication fraction is 100%, the same as case 2, but its replicated packet rate is 50% against 100% in case 2. The replicated packet rate cannot tell cases 2 and 3 apart, and the duplication fraction cannot tell cases 2 and 4 apart.

The order of arrival does not matter. Variations of case 2 such as (1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 3, 4) or (1, 2, 3, 4, 4, 3, 2, 1) give the same results.
sections.eli5: If every letter comes twice, the two numbers agree. If only half the letters come three times, the numbers split apart, which is why we keep both.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The memo does not specify an implementation, so it does not directly affect Internet security, but implementations must be mindful. The RFC names two worries. First, measurements are active and inject packets, so parameters MUST be chosen to add only trivial traffic. Too much traffic can skew results and, in extreme cases, cause congestion and denial of service.

Second, the measurements themselves can be harmed. Routers might give measurement traffic different priority from normal traffic, and an attacker injecting artificial measurement traffic that is accepted as legitimate would artificially lower the loss rate. Methodologies SHOULD therefore reduce the chance that measurement traffic can be told apart from normal traffic, and authentication such as digital signatures may be used against injected traffic.

Privacy concerns are limited because these are active measurements: unlike passive ones, there is no release of existing user data. Section 7 adds that IANA registered the metrics in the IPPM Metrics Registry of RFC 4148.
sections.eli5: Test packets should be few so they do not clog the road, and they should look like ordinary traffic so nobody can cheat the test.
